## What counts as spices

<a id="hmi-ing-001"></a>
<a id="what-commodity-biological-species-edible-part-and-commercial-forms-does-this-page-cover"></a>
<a id="hmi-ing-002"></a>
<a id="which-processing-states-and-derivatives-are-distinct-materials-rather-than-synonyms"></a>

<div class="hmi-analyte-explorer" id="hmi-occurrence-spices" data-analyte-explorer data-compact-intro="true" data-source-summaries="true"><details class="hmi-drawer-disclosure" data-explorer-context><summary data-open-context aria-haspopup="dialog" aria-controls="hmi-occurrence-spices-drawer">Comparison methods and scope</summary><div data-explorer-context-content>

<p>Each row is one statistic a source reports for one form of spices, group and metal; percentiles, ranges and maxima reported for the same samples as a mean or median are shown on that row. Different forms and preparation states are kept apart, and dry-weight results never share a reference with as-sold or fresh-weight results. Ratings place a result against an HMI reference built from monitoring results and ordinary-setting medians for the same form and basis. Same-study contrasts compare a contaminated or treated site with its control, targeted with random sampling, a prepared form with the unprocessed one, or one group of a study with the median of its other groups. Held rows failed a check against their own source and are shown but not compared.</p>

Each sampling family has equal total weight. Non-detects stay as zero-to-limit intervals, so quartiles carry lower and upper bounds. Means, ranges and maxima never enter as observations. At least four reference units and a definitely positive Q1 to Q3 spread are required. This is a display eligibility rule, not statistical validation.</p><p class="hmi-drawer-section-title" role="heading" aria-level="3">Limitations</p><p>8 sampling families with different designs; none is a probability sample of world supply. <a id="sources-and-contamination-pathways"></a>
## How metals reach spices

<a id="hmi-ing-010"></a>
<a id="what-evidence-supports-root-uptake-surface-deposition-feed-transfer-or-other-biological-pathways"></a>
<a id="hmi-ing-011"></a>

<a id="which-source-attribution-claims-are-measured-modelled-inferred-or-unresolved"></a>

The evidence on how metals reach spices comes from studies that compared exposed and ordinary settings. Spices, as sold from grown independently had total mercury higher at 8.7 µg/kg, against 6.17 µg/kg for all samples in the same study.<sup class="cite">[[sources/fischer2022-mercury-spice-plants-poland|7]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">Fischer A, Brodziak-Dopierała B · 2022</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/fischer2022-mercury-spice-plants-poland">The Mercury Concentration in Spice Plants</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">Processes</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/fischer2022-mercury-spice-plants-poland">Read source →</a></span></span></sup>

These are observational comparisons from single studies; the size of the difference depends on the site, metal and distance.

Spices, dried (EMRO) had lead lower at 23 µg/kg, against 120 µg/kg for the unprocessed form in the same group (spices, as sold).<sup class="cite">[[sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants|1]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">World Health Organization · 2026</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants">GEMS/Food Contaminants database heavy-metal exports</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">GEMS/Food Contamination Monitoring and Assessment Programme</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants">Read source →</a></span></span></sup> In another study, spices, flour or meal (ingredient for canned meatballs in tomato sauce) had cadmium lower at 10 µg/kg, against 70 µg/kg for the unprocessed form in the same group (spices, as sold).<sup class="cite">[[sources/stojanovic2021-serbia-canned-meat-tinplate-metals|16]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">Stojanović B, Janković S, Đorđević V, Marjanović S, Vasilev D, Stojanović Z, Balaban M, Antić V · 2021</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/stojanovic2021-serbia-canned-meat-tinplate-metals">Determination of toxic elements in meat products from Serbia packaged in tinplate cans</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">Research Square preprint, posted 26 February 2021 (version 1)</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/stojanovic2021-serbia-canned-meat-tinplate-metals">Read source →</a></span></span></sup>

Forms differ in water content, so a per-kilogram difference is not by itself a measured removal or gain of metal.

## Mitigation for spices

<a id="hmi-ing-019"></a>
<a id="which-prevention-mitigation-or-remediation-measures-have-been-evaluated-for-this-ingredient"></a>
<a id="hmi-ing-020"></a>

Lot testing against the applicable limit is the check that can be verified.

<p class="hmi-mitigation-gap" data-mitigation-gap>No measured way to lower metals in this food is in the library yet.</p>



<a id="trade-offs-and-failure-modes"></a>
## Trade-offs and limits of controls

<a id="hmi-ing-022"></a>
<a id="can-an-intervention-increase-another-contaminant-or-redistribute-contamination-to-a-by-product"></a>
<a id="hmi-ing-023"></a>
<a id="what-effects-on-nutrition-yield-sensory-quality-stability-and-waste-streams-were-measured"></a>
<a id="hmi-ing-024"></a>
<a id="what-costs-constraints-adverse-effects-or-failure-modes-are-documented-and-which-are-unknown"></a>

Avoiding exposed growing areas lowered the metal measured in the studies available, but no study measured the cost or supply effect of doing so.<sup class="cite">[[sources/fischer2022-mercury-spice-plants-poland|7]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">Fischer A, Brodziak-Dopierała B · 2022</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/fischer2022-mercury-spice-plants-poland">The Mercury Concentration in Spice Plants</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">Processes</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/fischer2022-mercury-spice-plants-poland">Read source →</a></span></span></sup> Metals do not move together, so a lot that passes a lead limit says little about cadmium, arsenic or nickel unless those are tested as well.

<a id="which-methods-species-measurements-validation-evidence-and-reporting-limits-are-needed"></a>
<a id="hmi-ing-027"></a>
<a id="what-can-a-certificate-of-analysis-or-non-detect-establish-and-what-remains-untested"></a>

Results depend on the method and its reporting limit. Reporting limits for lead ranged from 0.01 µg/kg (Lidiková et al. 2021) to 5,000 µg/kg (WHO GEMS/Food), so a non-detect from a less sensitive method says much less.<sup Every source record that names spices was decided on its content: 38 occurrence extracted, 38 records in all. The occurrence table renders every extracted result; held values remain visible with their reason.

References identify the sources used in these answers. The Sources index preserves additional discovery links; inclusion there does not mean a source has been reviewed for this assessment. Corrections, completed searches, new direct evidence and changes in requirements should reopen the relevant answer.


<a id="universal-faqs"></a>
## Spices FAQs

<details class="qa" data-hmi-faq="1" id="what-heavy-metals-are-found-in-spices" data-anchor="what-heavy-metals-are-found-in-spices" data-question="What heavy metals are found in spices?">
<summary><span class="mk" aria-hidden="true"></span>What heavy metals are found in spices?</summary>
<div class="ans" data-hmi-faq-answer="1">

The library reports lead, cadmium, total arsenic, inorganic arsenic, dimethylarsinic acid, total mercury, nickel, chromium, aluminium, tin, antimony, Co, Cu, Fe, Mn, Zn, V, Se, As, Be and Sr in spices, most often lead, cadmium and total arsenic.<sup class="cite">[[sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants|1]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">World Health Organization · 2026</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants">GEMS/Food Contaminants database heavy-metal exports</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">GEMS/Food Contamination Monitoring and Assessment Programme</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants">Read source →</a></span></span></sup><sup class="cite">[[sources/angelon-gaetz2018-lead-spices-north-carolina|2]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">Angelon-Gaetz KA, Klaus C, Chaudhry EA, Bean DK · 2018</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/angelon-gaetz2018-lead-spices-north-carolina">Lead in Spices, Herbal Remedies, and Ceremonial Powders Sampled from Home Investigations for Children with Elevated Blood Lead Levels — North Carolina, 2011–2018</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">MMWR Morbidity and Mortality Weekly Report</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/angelon-gaetz2018-lead-spices-north-carolina">Read source →</a></span></span></sup><sup class="cite">[[sources/ericson2020-georgian-spices-lead|3]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">Ericson B, Gabelaia L, Keith J, Kashibadze T, Beraia N, Sturua L, Kazzi Z · 2020</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/ericson2020-georgian-spices-lead">Elevated Levels of Lead (Pb) Identified in Georgian Spices</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">Annals of Global Health</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/ericson2020-georgian-spices-lead">Read source →</a></span></span></sup><sup class="cite">[[sources/fechner2022-bfr-meal-hg-cd-pb-ni-germany|4]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">Fechner C, Hackethal C, Höpfner T, Dietrich J, Bloch D, Lindtner O, Sarvan I · 2022</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/fechner2022-bfr-meal-hg-cd-pb-ni-germany">Results of the BfR MEAL Study: In Germany, mercury is mostly contained in fish and seafood while cadmium, lead, and nickel are present in a broad spectrum of foods</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">Food Chemistry: X</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/fechner2022-bfr-meal-hg-cd-pb-ni-germany">Read source →</a></span></span></sup> WHO GEMS/Food submissions reported lead in spices, as sold from 5,229 results in 5 reporting regions, with subgroup medians from 0.725 to 14,500 µg/kg.<sup class="cite">[[sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants|1]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">World Health Organization · 2026</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants">GEMS/Food Contaminants database heavy-metal exports</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">GEMS/Food Contamination Monitoring and Assessment Programme</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants">Read source →</a></span></span></sup>

</div>
</details>

<details class="qa" data-hmi-faq="1" id="how-do-heavy-metals-get-into-spices" data-anchor="how-do-heavy-metals-get-into-spices" data-question="How do heavy metals get into spices?">
<summary><span class="mk" aria-hidden="true"></span>How do heavy metals get into spices?</summary>
<div class="ans" data-hmi-faq-answer="1">

In the studies available, spices from contaminated or exposed settings carried more metal than spices from the same study’s control.<sup class="cite">[[sources/fischer2022-mercury-spice-plants-poland|7]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">Fischer A, Brodziak-Dopierała B · 2022</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/fischer2022-mercury-spice-plants-poland">The Mercury Concentration in Spice Plants</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">Processes</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/fischer2022-mercury-spice-plants-poland">Read source →</a></span></span></sup> Spices, as sold from grown independently had total mercury higher at 8.7 µg/kg, against 6.17 µg/kg for all samples in the same study.<sup class="cite">[[sources/fischer2022-mercury-spice-plants-poland|7]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">Fischer A, Brodziak-Dopierała B · 2022</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/fischer2022-mercury-spice-plants-poland">The Mercury Concentration in Spice Plants</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">Processes</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/fischer2022-mercury-spice-plants-poland">Read source →</a></span></span></sup>

</div>
</details>

<details class="qa" data-hmi-faq="1" id="which-regions-report-the-lowest-levels-in-spices" data-anchor="which-regions-report-the-lowest-levels-in-spices" data-question="Which regions report the lowest levels in spices?">
<summary><span class="mk" aria-hidden="true"></span>Which regions report the lowest levels in spices?</summary>
<div class="ans" data-hmi-faq-answer="1">

Among GEMS/Food reporting regions, spices, as sold had the lowest lead subgroup median in PAHO (0.725 µg/kg) and the highest in SEARO (6,000 µg/kg); reporting regions are markets, not growing areas.<sup class="cite">[[sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants|1]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">World Health Organization · 2026</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants">GEMS/Food Contaminants database heavy-metal exports</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">GEMS/Food Contamination Monitoring and Assessment Programme</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants">Read source →</a></span></span></sup> For cadmium, the lowest regional median was in PAHO (0.085 µg/kg) and the highest in EMRO (365 µg/kg).<sup class="cite">[[sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants|1]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">World Health Organization · 2026</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants">GEMS/Food Contaminants database heavy-metal exports</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">GEMS/Food Contamination Monitoring and Assessment Programme</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants">Read source →</a></span></span></sup>

</div>
</details>

<details class="qa" data-hmi-faq="1" id="does-processing-change-heavy-metals-in-spices" data-anchor="does-processing-change-heavy-metals-in-spices" data-question="Does processing change heavy metals in spices?">
<summary><span class="mk" aria-hidden="true"></span>Does processing change heavy metals in spices?</summary>
<div class="ans" data-hmi-faq-answer="1">

Only comparisons between forms in the same study are available, not before-and-after measurements of the same spices.<sup class="cite">[[sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants|1]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">World Health Organization · 2026</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants">GEMS/Food Contaminants database heavy-metal exports</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">GEMS/Food Contamination Monitoring and Assessment Programme</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants">Read source →</a></span></span></sup> Spices, dried (EMRO) had lead lower at 23 µg/kg, against 120 µg/kg for the unprocessed form in the same group (spices, as sold).<sup class="cite">[[sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants|1]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">World Health Organization · 2026</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants">GEMS/Food Contaminants database heavy-metal exports</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">GEMS/Food Contamination Monitoring and Assessment Programme</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants">Read source →</a></span></span></sup>

</div>
</details>

<details class="qa" data-hmi-faq="1" id="how-much-of-the-arsenic-in-spices-is-inorganic" data-anchor="how-much-of-the-arsenic-in-spices-is-inorganic" data-question="How much of the arsenic in spices is inorganic?">
<summary><span class="mk" aria-hidden="true"></span>How much of the arsenic in spices is inorganic?</summary>
<div class="ans" data-hmi-faq-answer="1">

Inorganic arsenic, the more toxic form, was measured in 15 results from 2 sources, far fewer than total arsenic.<sup class="cite">[[sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants|1]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">World Health Organization · 2026</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants">GEMS/Food Contaminants database heavy-metal exports</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">GEMS/Food Contamination Monitoring and Assessment Programme</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants">Read source →</a></span></span></sup><sup class="cite">[[sources/efsa2014-dietary-exposure-iAs|18]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">European Food Safety Authority (EFSA) · 2014</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/efsa2014-dietary-exposure-iAs">Dietary exposure to inorganic arsenic in the European population</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">EFSA Journal 2014;12(3):3597</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/efsa2014-dietary-exposure-iAs">Read source →</a></span></span></sup> European Food Safety Authority (EFSA) 2014 reported inorganic arsenic at 69.9 µg/kg (mean) in spices, as sold from European dietary-survey occurrence data.<sup class="cite">[[sources/efsa2014-dietary-exposure-iAs|18]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">European Food Safety Authority (EFSA) · 2014</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/efsa2014-dietary-exposure-iAs">Dietary exposure to inorganic arsenic in the European population</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">EFSA Journal 2014;12(3):3597</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/efsa2014-dietary-exposure-iAs">Read source →</a></span></span></sup>

</div>
</details>
